title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1 close toward III: Hague Colloquy grants no more than Pelagius — all stall refusing the grace that by infused faith and charity makes the good will
latin: Ultimo in loco Collocutores Hagienses audiantur, qui infusionem Divinae gratiae agnoscunt quidem quoad intellectum et affectus, in voluntate autem negant istiusmodi infusionem locum habere, ut quae natura sua libera sit ad volendum bonum vel malum. In hisce omnibus nihil video gratiae Divinae tribui quod Pelagius ipse non concessisset. Illam mentis illuminationem et affectuum accensionem, et hisce mediantibus propulsionem voluntatis, et potentiam ad bonum volendum, a gratia arcessit Pelagius; Verum, actione sua (absque omni dono infuso) bonam fieri, et vivificari voluntatem sua propria actione, vix tam clare asseveravit ipse Pelagius. Videtis jam quousque in agnitione gratiae Divinae processit Pelagius, cum Pelagianis et Semipelagianis, Arminius etiam cum sectatoribus suis: videtis etiam eos omnes ad eandem metam haerere, neque velle admittere illam efficacissimam gratiam, qua inspirata fide et charitate voluntatem bonam facit, sed illam solummodo, qua potens redditur ut sua actione bona evadat, si ipsa velit esse bona, agendo bene.
pass_a: Last let the Hague Colloquists be heard, who indeed acknowledge an infusion of Divine grace as to the intellect and the affections, but in the will deny that such infusion has place, as being by its nature free unto willing good or evil. In all these things I see nothing attributed unto Divine grace which Pelagius himself would not have granted. That illumination of the mind and kindling of the affections, and by these means the propulsion of the will, and power unto willing the good, Pelagius fetches from grace; but that by its own action (without any infused gift) it becomes good, and that the will is quickened by its own proper action, Pelagius himself scarcely asserted so clearly. Ye see now how far Pelagius has proceeded in acknowledging Divine grace, with the Pelagians and Semipelagians, Arminius also with his followers: ye see also that they all stick at the same mark, and will not admit that most efficacious grace which, faith and charity being inspired, makes the good will, but only that by which it is made able to become good by its own action, if it itself will to be good, by doing well.
pass_b: Last hear the Hague Colloquists: they grant infusion of divine grace as to intellect and affections, but deny such infusion in the will, as free by nature to will good or evil. In all this I see nothing credited to divine grace that Pelagius himself would not have granted. Mind’s illumination, kindling of affections, and by these a push on the will and power to will the good—Pelagius fetches from grace; but that the will becomes good by its own act without any infused gift, and is quickened by its own act, even Pelagius scarcely said so clearly. See how far Pelagius, with Pelagians and Semipelagians, and Arminius with his followers, go in owning divine grace—and see them all stuck at the same mark, refusing the most efficacious grace that, faith and charity inspired, makes the good will, and admitting only the grace that makes the will able to become good by its own doing, if it wills to be good by doing well.

lemmas.gloss: Hague: no infusion in the will
refuse grace that makes the good will

title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1.III: the Grace of Christ the Fathers pressed is what Pelagius and Arminius explode as free will’s coercive — Bishop of Salisbury De vera grat. Christi p.60
latin: III. Veniamus ad illud quod in hac prima propositione nostra restat explicandum; Qualis nimirum fuerit ea gratia, quam Augustinus una cum reliquis Orthodoxis a Pelagio agnosci contendebant, quamque per excellentiam Gratiam Christi indigitabant. Affirmamus autem, non aliam fuisse quam hanc quam Pelagius et Arminius quasi liberi arbitrii coactivum exploserunt. Non possumus autem eam aptioribus vocabulis depingere, quam depicta est a Reverendo Episcopo Sarisburiensi, De vera grat. Christi, pag. 60. Haec, inquit ille, est vera gratia, quam Christiana fides agnoscit et credit, qua Deus dat leges suas in mentes nostras, et in cordibus nostris inscribit eas; qua ubi requirit voluntatem nostram, facit ipse ut velimus; ubi converti jubet, facit simul ut convertamur; ubi fidem postulat, facit dono suo ut credamus.
pass_a: III. Let us come unto that which remains to be unfolded in this our first proposition; namely, What that grace was which Augustine together with the rest of the Orthodox contended should be acknowledged by Pelagius, and which they pointed out by excellence as the Grace of Christ. But we affirm it was no other than this which Pelagius and Arminius exploded as free will’s coercive. Nor can we depict it in fitter words than it is depicted by the Reverend Bishop of Salisbury, De vera grat. Christi, pag. 60. This, he says, is the true grace which Christian faith acknowledges and believes, by which God gives his laws into our minds, and inscribes them in our hearts; by which, where he requires our will, he himself makes that we will; where he commands to be converted, he makes at once that we are converted; where he demands faith, he makes by his gift that we believe.
pass_b: III. What remains in this first proposition: what grace Augustine with the other Orthodox contended Pelagius must acknowledge—and which they named by excellence the Grace of Christ. We affirm it was none other than the grace Pelagius and Arminius explode as free will’s coercive. We cannot paint it in fitter words than the Reverend Bishop of Salisbury (De vera gratia Christi, p. 60): This is the true grace Christian faith owns and believes, by which God gives his laws into our minds and writes them on our hearts; by which, when he requires our will, he himself makes us will; when he bids convert, he makes us convert at once; when he demands faith, by his gift he makes us believe.

lemmas.lemma: Episcopo Sarisburiensi ... facit ipse ut velimus

title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1.III: Augustine — true grace is inspiration of love; he makes us walk and do; adjutorium whereby something is done; not only to be able but to will
latin: Ex Augustino paucula delibemus: Contra 2. Epist. Pelag. lib. 4. cap. 5. gratiam veram sic describit, Inspiratio dilectionis, ut cognita sancto amore faciamus, propria gratia est. Et cap. 6. Nos ambulamus, nos observamus, nos facimus, sed ille facit ut ambulemus, ut observemus, ut faciamus. Haec est gratia Dei bonos faciens nos, haec misericordia ejus praeveniens nos. Hanc gratiam Christi vocat adjutorium quo aliquid fit. Dicit ab hac gratia esse in nobis non solum posse quod volumus, verum etiam velle quod possumus, De corr. et grat. cap. 11. et 12.
pass_a: From Augustine we will taste a few things: Contra 2. Epist. Pelag. lib. 4. cap. 5. he thus describes true grace, The inspiration of love, that we may do what is known with holy love, is proper grace. And cap. 6. We walk, we observe, we do, but he makes that we walk, that we observe, that we do. This is the grace of God making us good, this his mercy preventing us. This grace of Christ he calls a help whereby something is done. He says that from this grace there is in us not only to be able to do what we will, but also to will what we can, De corr. et grat. cap. 11. and 12.
pass_b: A few from Augustine (Contra duas epistolas Pelagianorum 4.5): he describes true grace as the inspiration of love, that we may do what is known with holy love—that is proper grace. And 4.6: We walk, we keep, we do—but he makes us walk, keep, do. This is God’s grace making us good; this his mercy going before us. He calls this grace of Christ a help whereby something is done. From it, he says, there is in us not only power to do what we will, but also to will what we can (De correptione et gratia 11–12).

lemmas.lemma: non solum posse ... verum etiam velle
lemmas.gloss: grace gives willing, not mere ability

title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1.III: grace that only warns and persuades, leaving the will under free will’s dice, is law not proper grace — Aug. De grat. Christi 13–14
latin: De illa autem gratia quae monet et suadet tantum, sed ipsam Voluntatem quasi sub alea incerta liberi sui arbitrii relinquit, sentit Augustinus, ad legem potius eam spectare quam ad gratiam proprie dictam: Qui novit quid fieri debeat, et non facit, nondum a Deo didicit secundum gratiam, sed secundum legem, De gratia Christi, contra Pelag. cap. 13. Et initio cap. 14. Qui non venit, nondum ille recte dicitur didicisse: audivit quidem et didicit oportere veniendum, sed facere non vult quod didicit. Prorsus non recte dicitur de isto docendi modo, quo per gratiam docet Deus.
pass_a: But concerning that grace which only warns and persuades, but leaves the Will itself as it were under the uncertain dice of its free will, Augustine judges that it looks rather unto law than unto grace properly so called: He who knows what ought to be done, and does not, has not yet learned from God according to grace, but according to law, De gratia Christi, contra Pelag. cap. 13. And at the beginning of cap. 14. He who has not come is not yet rightly said to have learned: he has indeed heard and learned that one ought to come, but he wills not to do what he has learned. It is by no means rightly said of that mode of teaching by which God teaches through grace.
pass_b: But of the grace that only warns and persuades, and leaves the will under free will’s uncertain dice, Augustine holds it looks to law rather than to grace properly so called (De gratia Christi contra Pelagium 13): Who knows what ought to be done and does not, has not yet learned from God according to grace, but according to law. And at the start of 14: Who has not come is not yet rightly said to have learned—he heard and learned that he ought to come, but will not do what he learned. That mode of teaching is not rightly called the way God teaches by grace.

lemmas.lemma: ad legem potius ... quam ad gratiam

title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1.III: not Augustine alone — Milevis can. 4, African exiles, Orange can. 4 preach creating/vivifying grace that works both to will and to do
latin: Sed dixerit aliquis, Haec fuit singularis Augustini sententia, in quam absolutae praedestinationis opinio eum pertraxit. Imo fuit omnium Orthodoxorum communis, ut ex Conciliis contra Pelagium et Semipelagianos celebratis constat. Ex Milevitano, canone 4, Per gratiam Christi nobis praestatur, ut quod faciendum cognoverimus, etiam facere diligamus atque valeamus. Paulo post, Utrumque donum Dei est, et scire quid facere debeamus, et diligere ut faciamus. Ex Epistola Synodica Episcoporum Africanorum in Sardinia exsulum idem patet: Jubet Deus homini ut velit, sed Dominus in homine operatur et velle: jubet ut faciat, sed operatur et facere. Deus in vivificandis hominibus nullum initium humanae voluntatis exspectat, sed ipsam voluntatem bonam faciendo vivificat. Demum ex Concilio Arausicano idem liquet; canone 4, Si quis, ut a peccato purgemur, voluntatem nostram Deum exspectare contendit, non autem ut etiam purgari velimus per Sancti Spiritus infusionem et operationem in nos fieri confitetur, resistit ipsi Spiritui Sancto per Solomonem dicenti, Praeparatur voluntas a Domino, et Apostolo salubriter praedicanti, Deus est qui operatur in nobis et velle et perficere pro bona sua voluntate.
pass_a: But someone will say, This was Augustine’s singular sentence, into which the opinion of absolute predestination drew him. Nay, it was common unto all the Orthodox, as is plain from the Councils celebrated against Pelagius and the Semipelagians. From the Milevitan, canon 4, By the grace of Christ it is granted unto us that what we have known ought to be done, we also love and are able to do. A little after, Both are God’s gift, both to know what we ought to do, and to love that we may do. From the Synodical Epistle of the African Bishops exiled in Sardinia the same is plain: God commands a man that he will, but the Lord works in the man also to will: he commands that he do, but works also to do. God in quickening men waits for no beginning of the human will, but quickens by making the good will itself. Finally from the Council of Orange the same is clear; canon 4, If anyone contends that God waits for our will that we may be purged from sin, and does not confess that even our willing to be purged is wrought in us by the infusion and operation of the Holy Spirit, he resists the Holy Spirit himself speaking through Solomon, The will is prepared by the Lord, and the Apostle wholesomely preaching, It is God who works in us both to will and to finish according to his good will.
pass_b: Someone will say this was Augustine’s private view, pulled in by absolute predestination. No: it was common to all the Orthodox, as the anti-Pelagian councils show. Milevis canon 4: By Christ’s grace it is granted us that what we know ought to be done, we also love and can do. A little later: Both are God’s gift—to know what we ought to do, and to love so that we do. The synodical letter of the African bishops exiled in Sardinia is the same: God commands a man to will, but the Lord works in the man also to will; he commands to do, but works also to do. In quickening men God waits for no start of the human will; he quickens by making the good will itself. Orange canon 4 is clear: If anyone contends God waits for our will so we may be purged from sin, and does not confess that even our willing to be purged is wrought in us by the Spirit’s infusion and working, he resists the Holy Spirit speaking through Solomon, The will is prepared by the Lord, and the Apostle, It is God who works in us both to will and to finish according to his good will.

lemmas.gloss: Milevis: grace gives loving and being able
Orange 4: will prepared by the Lord

title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1 close: illuminating/exciting grace is not the Grace of Christ Orthodoxy pressed — that grace creates the good will; received grace is not wage of a non-resisting will
latin: Quorsum haec tam multa de gratia Christi? Ut intelligatur, Ex communi consensu Orthodoxorum, gratiam illam illuminatricem, monitricem, et excitatricem, quae nulli mortalium deest (si credimus Arminianis) quaeque effectu salutifero in plurimis caret, non esse eam gratiam Christi, ad cujus agnitionem Pelagium adigere Orthodoxi voluerunt; sed eam quae voluntatem bonam creat, hominem sanctificat, ac denique effectum salutis infallibiliter producit. Hunc esse sensum hujus vocabuli non latuit Magistrum Sententiarum, lib. 2. dist. 26. lit. D. Gratia, inquit, voluntatem praeveniens et praeparans, est fides cum dilectione. Hanc etiam gratiam intellexit Aquinas, 1. 2. qu. 111. art. 3. quando quinque effecta ei assignavit, nempe, ut anima sanetur, ut bonum velit, ut bonum quod vult operetur, ut in bono perseveret, ut ad gloriam perveniat. Maneat ergo hoc fixum et stabilitum, Gratiam Christi receptam non esse mercedem voluntatis non-resistentis, sed non-resistentem voluntatem esse effectum hujus gratiae donatae ac receptae. Atque haec ad primae propositionis explicationem abunde sufficiant.
pass_a: To what end so many things concerning the grace of Christ? That it may be understood that, From the common consent of the Orthodox, that illuminating, admonishing, and exciting grace, which is wanting unto no mortal (if we believe the Arminians) and which in very many lacks a saving effect, is not that grace of Christ unto whose acknowledgment the Orthodox willed to drive Pelagius; but that which creates the good will, sanctifies the man, and at length infallibly produces the effect of salvation. That this is the sense of this word was not hidden from the Master of the Sentences, lib. 2. dist. 26. lit. D. Grace, he says, preventing and preparing the will, is faith with love. This grace also Aquinas understood, 1. 2. qu. 111. art. 3. when he assigned five effects unto it, namely, that the soul be healed, that it will the good, that it work the good it wills, that it persevere in the good, that it arrive unto glory. Let this therefore remain fixed and established, that the received Grace of Christ is not the wage of a non-resisting will, but that the non-resisting will is the effect of this grace given and received. And these things abundantly suffice unto the unfolding of the first proposition.
pass_b: Why so much on the grace of Christ? So it is clear from Orthodox common consent: the illuminating, warning, exciting grace that—if Arminians are believed—fails no mortal, yet in many lacks a saving effect, is not the Grace of Christ to whose acknowledgment the Orthodox meant to drive Pelagius. That grace creates the good will, sanctifies the man, and at last infallibly produces salvation’s effect. The Master of the Sentences knew this sense (lib. 2, dist. 26, lit. D): Grace preventing and preparing the will is faith with love. So Aquinas (1a2ae q.111 a.3) when he assigned it five effects: that the soul be healed, will the good, work the good it wills, persevere in the good, and reach glory. Let this stand fixed: received Grace of Christ is not the wage of a non-resisting will; the non-resisting will is the effect of that grace given and received. Enough for the first proposition.

lemmas.gloss: Christ’s grace creates will and saves

title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 2 open: this Grace of Christ was prepared from eternity and given in time to some, to others neither — event proves; ‘given to all but not all receive’ fails
latin: Transeo ad secundam: Ea fuit hujusmodi; Haec gratia Christi quibusdam praeparata fuit ab aeterno et donata in tempore, quibusdam nec praeparata nec donata. Hic multis verbis haud opus est, nam res ipsa loquitur. Videmus siquidem ex eventu non dari omnibus praedictam gratiam efficacem; et quibus nunquam fuit data, iis ex aeterno Dei beneplacito nunquam fuisse praeparatam, extra omnem dubitationis aleam ponendum est. Quis autem tam excors ut dicat fidem et charitatem omnibus donari et infundi? aut bonam voluntatem in omnibus creari? aut perseverantiam et gloriam omnibus concedi? Neque hic locum habere potest illa exceptio, Deus haec dat omnibus; sed omnes non accipiunt. Nam cuicunque data est a Deo bona voluntas, fides, charitas, perseverantia, ille haec omnia accepisse praesumitur. Donata enim dicuntur, non illis qui talibus donis carent, sed qui iisdem gaudent.
pass_a: I pass unto the second: It was of this sort; This grace of Christ was prepared for certain ones from eternity and given in time, for certain ones neither prepared nor given. Here there is by no means need of many words, for the thing itself speaks. For we see from the event that the foresaid efficacious grace is not given unto all; and that unto those unto whom it was never given, it was never prepared from God’s eternal good pleasure, is to be set outside every cast of doubt. But who is so witless as to say that faith and charity are given and infused unto all? or that a good will is created in all? or that perseverance and glory are granted unto all? Nor can that exception have place here, God gives these unto all; but all do not receive. For untowhomsoever a good will, faith, charity, perseverance has been given by God, he is presumed to have received all these. For they are said to be given, not unto those who lack such gifts, but unto those who rejoice in the same.
pass_b: I pass to the second: This grace of Christ was prepared from eternity and given in time to some; to others neither prepared nor given. Few words are needed—the thing speaks. From the event we see that efficacious grace is not given to all; and that for those never given it, it was never prepared from God’s eternal good pleasure, is beyond doubt. Who is so witless as to say faith and charity are given and infused to all, or a good will created in all, or perseverance and glory granted to all? Nor does the dodge hold: God gives these to all, but all do not receive. Whoever God has given a good will, faith, charity, perseverance is presumed to have received them all. Gifts are said to be given not to those who lack them, but to those who enjoy them.

lemmas.lemma: Deus haec dat omnibus; sed omnes non accipiunt

title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 2: Augustine restricts vivifying grace to the predestined and purpose-called — De grat. Christi 12–13; De praedest. sanct. 9; faith a gift to some not all
latin: Sed videamus quae fuerit hac de re Orthodoxorum sententia. Ex Augustino habemus infinita paene testimonia. Praeclarum est illud, De gratia Christi contra Pelag. et Caelestium, cap. 12. et 13. Haec gratia qua virtus in infirmitate perficitur, praedestinatos et secundum propositum vocatos ad summam perfectionem glorificationisque perducit. Hanc gratiam Deus altius et interius cum ineffabili suavitate infundit, non solum per eos qui plantant et rigant extrinsecus, sed etiam per seipsum, qui incrementum suum ministrat occultus, ita ut non ostendat tantummodo veritatem, verum etiam impertiat charitatem. Hisce verbis hanc gratiam ad praedestinatos et secundum propositum vocatos restringit, atque simul ostendit, non esse efficacem ex eventu solummodo, sed ex proposito dantis, et ex ipsa datae gratiae natura. Talem gratiam omnibus non dari, meridiana luce clarius est. Non minus illustre est illud alterum testimonium, De praedest. sanctor. cap. 8. Fides inchoata et perfecta donum Dei est: et hoc donum quibusdam dari, quibusdam non dari, omnino non dubitet qui non vult manifestissimis sacris literis repugnare.
pass_a: But let us see what was the Orthodox sentence concerning this matter. From Augustine we have almost infinite testimonies. Excellent is that, De gratia Christi contra Pelag. et Caelestium, cap. 12. and 13. This grace whereby strength is perfected in weakness leads the predestinated and those called according to purpose unto the highest perfection and glorification. This grace God pours in more deeply and inwardly with ineffable sweetness, not only through those who plant and water outwardly, but also through himself, who secretly ministers his increase, so that he not only shows the truth, but also imparts charity. By these words he restricts this grace unto the predestinated and those called according to purpose, and at once shows that it is not efficacious from the event only, but from the purpose of the giver, and from the nature of the grace given. That such grace is not given unto all is clearer than noonday light. No less illustrious is that other testimony, De praedest. sanctor. cap. 8. Faith begun and perfected is God’s gift: and that this gift is given unto certain, not given unto certain, let him by no means doubt who wills not to contradict the most manifest sacred letters.
pass_b: What was the Orthodox view? From Augustine we have almost endless witnesses. Excellent is De gratia Christi contra Pelagium et Caelestium 12–13: This grace whereby strength is perfected in weakness leads the predestined and those called according to purpose to the highest perfection and glorification. God pours this grace in more deeply and inwardly with unspeakable sweetness—not only through those who plant and water outwardly, but through himself, who secretly gives the increase—so that he not only shows the truth but imparts charity. So he restricts this grace to the predestined and purpose-called, and shows it is efficacious not from the event alone but from the giver’s purpose and the nature of the grace given. That such grace is not given to all is clearer than noon. No less clear is De praedestinatione sanctorum 8: Faith begun and perfected is God’s gift; and that this gift is given to some and not to others, let no one doubt who will not contradict the plainest Scripture.

lemmas.lemma: Fides ... quibusdam dari, quibusdam non dari
